newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, bonds rise on data, dollar jumps vs mark.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds rise on data, dollar jumps vs mark.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks and bonds jumped on Tuesday as key manufacturing data eased concerns about a near-term rise in interest rates.
The dollar rose to its highest level against the German mark in over three years after top U.S. and German officials voiced confidence in the strength of the U.S. currency.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended 49.54 points higher at 7,722.33.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,691 to 1,133 on active volume of 544 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

The good news came from the National Association of Purchasing Management's (NAPM) monthly survey, which showed an increase in manufacturing activity in June, though at a slower pace than economists had expected.
The data soothed recent jitters over the Federal Reserve's interest rate policy meeting, which began Tuesday and concludes on Wednesday.
"I don't think anybody's scared at this point," said Arnie Owen, managing director of capital markets at Cruttenden Roth. "I certainly don't think anyone sees any inflation out there."

The bond market also shot higher on the NAPM report, sending the yield on the benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury up 18/32, or $5.625 on a $1,000 bond, lowering its yield to 6.74 percent from 6.79 percent Monday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
Stocks quickly followed, led by interest rate-sensitive sectors like finance and transportation.
While Wall Street is nearly unanimous in expecting the Fed will leave interest rates steady, it still faces a critical test in the monthly data on payrolls and wages.
The report is due out Thursday instead of its traditional Friday release because of the Independence Day-shortened work week.
The dollar rose to a 40-month peak of 1.7488 marks during European trading and ended at 1.7468, slightly up from 1.7455 late Monday.
The dollar also advanced against the yen, climbing in overseas trade after a sharp fall in the Japanese stock market, and closed at 114.90 yen against 114.63 late Monday.
Soybean prices fell on talk that imports from Brazil will ease tight supplies in the United States before an expected record soybean crop is harvested in the Midwest this fall.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybeans for July delivery plummeted 39 cents a bushel to close at $7.32.

The heavy selling in soybeans helped push down corn prices, with July corn ending down 4-3/4 cents a bushel at $2.43-1/4. July wheat closed 1-1/4 cents a bushel lower at $3.22-1/2, under pressure from newly arriving winter wheat supplies as harvest gets under way in the upper Midwest.
In New York, gold prices tested new four-year lows but platinum group metals ended little changed.
Gold for August delivery at the COMEX ended down 20 cents at $335.10 an ounce, holding above the life-of-contract low at $334.60 set on Monday.
Oil prices also rose, fuelled by an expected decline in petroleum inventories and delays in Iraqi oil sales.
Crude oil for August delivery closed 32 cents higher at $20.12 a barrel, with August gasoline closing up 0.66 cent a gallon at 58.78 cents and August heating oil up 0.99 cent a gallon at 54.84 cents.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 closed at 4,728.3, up 123.7 points, or 2.69 percent. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average closed at 20,175.52, down 429.44 points, or 2.08 percent.
